For satellites in LEO (altitudes below 1,600 km [1,000 miles]), travel time is much shorter, but, unlike satellites in geostationary orbit that remain over the same spot, satellites in LEO pass over a specific spot for only a few minutes. To maintain constant service, many satellites are needed in one orbit so that as one is setting, another is rising. ASML Holding will report third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, October 14, giving investors a critical look at whether demand for the company’s advanced lithography systems remains strong enough to support its premium valuation.
The Dutch semiconductor-equipment company has become one of the largest beneficiaries of the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. Its extreme ultraviolet lithography machines are essential for manufacturing the most advanced processors produced by TSMC, Samsung and Intel.
ASML’s US-listed shares finished Friday at approximately $1,780 after gaining 0.6%. The stock has risen sharply as semiconductor manufacturers expanded capacity for AI accelerators, high-bandwidth memory and advanced logic chips.
The challenge is that the market already expects exceptional growth. Reported revenue will matter, but ASML’s order intake and guidance for 2027 could have an even greater influence on the stock’s post-earnings direction.
ASML will release its third-quarter results at 7:00 a.m. Central European Time on Wednesday, October 14. Management will hold a 60-minute investor call at 3:00 p.m. CET.
The report will arrive before the US stock market opens and on the same day as the September US Consumer Price Index. That combination could produce significant volatility in ASML shares, with earnings driving company-specific expectations and CPI affecting Treasury yields and technology-sector valuations.
ASML previously forecast third-quarter revenue between €11 billion and €12 billion, representing a substantial sequential increase from €9.33 billion in the second quarter.
Market estimates point to revenue of approximately €11.66 billion, or roughly $13.2 billion at recent exchange rates. Consensus estimates for the US-listed shares place earnings near $12.47 per share, although figures vary between providers because ASML reports its results in euros.

ASML expects Installed Base Management revenue, which includes service and equipment upgrades, to reach approximately €2.9 billion. This recurring business is important because its margins can exceed those generated by new systems and it benefits from the expanding number of ASML machines operating at customer factories.
Quarterly revenue largely reflects equipment that was ordered months or years earlier. Net bookings provide a more forward-looking view of demand and may therefore determine whether investors view the report as strong or disappointing.
ASML is the only company capable of producing EUV lithography systems at commercial scale. These machines use extremely short wavelengths of light to print the intricate patterns required for advanced semiconductors.
Low-NA EUV systems are already essential for leading-edge logic chips and advanced memory. ASML’s newer High-NA EUV platform is designed to support smaller, denser and more powerful chips at future manufacturing nodes.

ASML said in July that customer commitments were strengthening across its product portfolio and that order intake had remained exceptionally strong during the first half of 2026.
A third-quarter increase in EUV bookings would reinforce the argument that AI infrastructure investment is translating into long-term equipment demand rather than a temporary surge in orders.
A weaker booking figure would not necessarily indicate collapsing demand because orders can be uneven from one quarter to another. However, cautious customer commentary or delays in 2027 capacity plans would raise more substantial concerns.
ASML reported second-quarter revenue of €9.33 billion, above its guidance, while net income reached €2.92 billion. Earnings were €7.59 per share.
The company sold 86 new lithography systems and five used systems during the quarter. Installed Base Management revenue reached €2.76 billion, exceeding management’s forecast and helping the gross margin rise to 54%.
Following those results, ASML increased its full-year revenue forecast to between €43 billion and €45 billion. It also raised its expected annual gross margin to between 54% and 56%.
The updated outlook was substantially above the approximately €39.6 billion analysts had expected before the announcement. Management attributed the increase to accelerating investment in advanced logic and memory capacity.
For the third quarter, investors will examine whether ASML maintains that guidance or raises it again. An increase in the lower end of the annual revenue range would be especially supportive because it would imply strong fourth-quarter shipments and service revenue.
High-NA EUV represents one of the most important components of ASML’s long-term growth case.
The next-generation machines provide higher resolution than the existing EUV platform, potentially reducing the number of production steps required to manufacture advanced chips. Each system can cost as much as $400 million, making High-NA adoption important for both revenue growth and average selling prices.
ASML reached a significant milestone during the second quarter when Intel qualified High-NA EUV for selected Intel 18A product layers. The company said its installed fleet was supporting customer development while additional production applications were being prepared.
Investors will want updates on:
A faster High-NA adoption schedule could support ASML’s valuation by increasing revenue per system and strengthening the company’s technological lead. Delays would create concern that customers can continue using conventional EUV with multiple patterning for longer than expected.
ASML currently expects low-NA EUV capacity of approximately 65 systems in 2026. It plans to expand that capacity by around 30% in 2027 and is studying another 30% increase for 2028.
The company has announced similar plans for deep ultraviolet immersion systems, with capacity expected to increase from approximately 130 units in 2026.
Management indicated that ASML was already close to receiving all the EUV orders needed to fill its 2027 capacity and had accumulated substantial commitments for 2028.
This visibility is central to the bullish case. ASML does not merely benefit from quarterly chip demand; it benefits when manufacturers commit years in advance to new factories and manufacturing nodes.
The expansion also introduces execution risks. EUV machines contain extremely complex components supplied by a limited number of specialized manufacturers. Zeiss is ASML’s exclusive source for several critical optical systems, making supplier capacity an important constraint.
US and Dutch export restrictions prevent ASML from selling its most advanced EUV systems to China and increasingly limit shipments of certain DUV equipment.
China’s contribution to ASML’s system sales reportedly declined from 36% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to approximately 19% in the second quarter of 2026.
Strong demand from TSMC, Samsung, SK Hynix, Intel and Micron has so far helped offset the decline. However, further restrictions on servicing installed machines or exporting additional DUV systems could create another revenue headwind.
Investors should watch management’s forecast for China’s full-year sales contribution and any discussion of new export rules. They should also monitor whether non-Chinese customers are ordering enough DUV equipment to replace lost regional demand.
Competition from Chinese lithography developers remains another long-term issue. China has made progress in older DUV technologies, but analysts generally believe local suppliers remain far behind ASML in EUV systems and advanced commercial production.
ASML shares enter earnings near $1,780. A compilation of analyst forecasts places the average 12-month price target at approximately $2,085, implying potential upside of about 17%, although targets range from $1,200 to $2,623.

The principal downside scenario would combine weaker bookings with cautious comments about 2027 customer capital expenditure. A gross margin below 55% or rising costs related to capacity expansion could also pressure the shares.
ASML’s valuation assumes that AI demand will remain strong for several years. As a result, meeting quarterly estimates may not be enough. Investors need evidence that current orders are converting into a durable backlog extending through 2027 and 2028.

articles.title: Airtel Business CEO backs AI regulation, says guardrails can unlock productivity gains - ET Enterprise AI
articles.summary: Airtel Business CEO backs AI regulation, says guardrails can unlock productivity gains  ET Enterprise AI
articles.full_text:
Airtel is committed to compliant practices that enhance productivity through AI. Sinha emphasized the growth of cybersecurity services in response to emerging digital threats. The company aims to deliver safe experiences for both enterprise and consumer segments.
On the government's plan to soon release a consultation paper on AI regulation dealing with issues like tech safety, deepfakes and a human-first approach, Sinha said it was "a step in the right direction".
"We work very closely with both government regulators, as well as our customers, to make sure that whatever we do is compliant, and we play a positive role in bringing out such specifications. So, that will continue to be our effort," he told PTI.
Airtel, he added, "will be playing a positive and active role in that".
Last week, IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the government, in a month's time, will bring a consultation paper on AI regulations, which will focus on key aspects such as AI safety, deepfakes and a human-first approach.
The consultation paper will form the base for AI regulations, Vaishnaw had said, adding that the time has come for India to have such a framework.
On the global debate surrounding AI, the Airtel Business CEO noted that as is the case with any technology, even for artificial intelligence, having tools or AI agents with the right guardrails and building an enterprise architecture that enables their safe deployment will ensure productivity gains.
"It is like any technology. If you deploy artificial intelligence or AI agents with the right guardrails, and if your enterprise architecture is built so that they can be safely deployed, you can get all the essential productivity gains for it. We ourselves, as an enterprise, are heavy users of that," Sinha said.
As the technology evolves, so would the architecture and methodology of safely deploying them, he said, adding that "I think that's the way to go".
It is pertinent to mention here that concern over rogue AI agents has grown in recent months. Reports of agents slipping out of test environments and acting beyond their mandates have drawn warnings from researchers, industry leaders and global experts, who say existing safeguards are not keeping pace with frontier model capabilities and are calling for layered controls and closer monitoring.
AI adoption would drive demand for reliable digital infrastructure, combining cloud services, data centres, connectivity, guardrails and cybersecurity, Sinha noted.
He said Airtel expected cloud, cybersecurity, Internet of Things, next-generation connectivity and communications-platform-as-a-service offerings to be among its growth drivers over the next three years.
He said the cybersecurity business was growing rapidly, with Airtel extending its offerings beyond traditional security services to address emerging digital threats.
The company has also expanded its consumer-focused fraud prevention capabilities, building on its spam prevention solution launched slightly over a year ago.
"When it comes to consumer business, we launched spam prevention slightly over a year ago, and over a period of time, based on the same technology that leverages network AI, we have created a fraud prevention solution.
"We also classify that within the cyber security category, and in the case of India, it becomes very relevant because almost half of the world's digital financial transactions happen in India, thanks to UPI, which also means digital frauds associated with that are also on the rise," he said.
Sinha said frauds on Airtel's telecom networks "dramatically decreased" since the launch of its spam prevention solution.
"It is a known fact that since we launched our spam prevention solution, frauds on Airtel's telecom networks have dramatically decreased. So, we continue to add that to our whole proposition of providing a safe experience to our customers, both in enterprise and in consumer space," he said.
Airtel Business, the enterprise unit of Bharti Airtel, sells connectivity, sovereign cloud, data centre, cyber security, IoT and cloud communications services to companies.

articles.full_text:
Microsoft is ready to pay MacBook owners to switch to its new Surface Laptop Ultra. The company is offering MacBook Pro owners up to $1,000 in promotional cash back on top of their trade-in value when they preorder the new laptop.
The cash back is paid on top of the standard trade-in value rather than being deducted from the purchase price at checkout. To receive cash back, buyers must purchase a qualifying Surface Laptop Ultra and submit an online trade-in claim with proof of purchase. After Microsoft’s trade-in partner receives and evaluates the MacBook, the customer receives its trade-in value plus any promotional cash back they qualify for.
The deal runs through November 23 in the US and Canada. The MacBook must meet Microsoft’s condition requirements and be mailed within 15 days of completing the trade-in process. The promotional bonus varies based on the device and its trade-in value, up to the advertised $1,000 maximum.
The Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599.99, making it the least expensive laptop in the RTX Spark lineup. Microsoft is positioning the machine as a high-performance option for power users, with Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform featuring an 18-core or 20-core CPU, an RTX GPU with up to 6,144 CUDA cores, and 24GB to 128GB of unified memory. Other highlights include a mini-LED display and a wide selection of ports, including a proprietary magnetic USB-C port.
The trade-in value itself varies depending on the MacBook Pro model and its condition. The source reports that the highest estimate it obtained from Microsoft’s website was $2,115 for a 16-inch MacBook Pro from 2025 equipped with 128GB of RAM and a 4TB SSD. Adding the maximum $1,000 promotional bonus could bring the total value to $3,115, although the final amount depends on the device and its eligibility for the offer.
The offer is a clear attempt to attract customers from Apple's premium laptop lineup. Rather than competing only on hardware and performance, Microsoft is giving MacBook Pro owners a financial incentive to switch platforms.
Preorders for the Surface Laptop Ultra are available through Microsoft’s website and Best Buy, with shipments set to begin on October 16.

articles.summary: INFQ Stock Surges After Infleqtion Solves Key Technical Hurdle In Large-Scale Quantum Computing  Stocktwits
articles.full_text:
Infleqtion shares surged 3.4% on Thursday and extended the climb overnight after the quantum computing company announced it had successfully entangled 30 logical qubits using just 80 physical qubits, marking a key milestone for its quantum computing platform.
The company unveiled the achievement at the Quantum World Congress 2026, saying it is the first neutral-atom quantum computing company to reach 30 logical qubits on a commercial system.
The milestone is significant because physical qubits are highly vulnerable to environmental noise and errors, while logical qubits use multiple physical qubits and software-based error-correction techniques to create more reliable quantum information.
Infleqtion said its 30 logical qubits were entangled into a single coherent quantum state, with the signal measuring approximately 1,000 times stronger than the underlying noise.
In a statement Thursday, the company said the result validates the architecture of its Sqale quantum processing platform and Superstaq software, while demonstrating the benefits of designing quantum hardware and software together.
An AI-assisted discovery also helped Infleqtion cut the number of physical gates required for a key logical operation by half. Quantum gates are the basic operations used to manipulate quantum information, so reducing the number required can help limit errors and improve system efficiency.
For the broader quantum computing industry, the achievement highlights a central challenge in moving from experimental machines to commercially useful systems: improving how efficiently physical qubits can be converted into reliable logical qubits.
The announcement comes as Infleqtion expands its commercial and government business.
In August, the company reported second-quarter revenue of $12.6 million, up 116%, and raised its 2026 revenue outlook. Infleqtion said it secured a proposed up to $100 million U.S. Commerce Department funding agreement, three Department of Energy Genesis Mission projects and a contract to deploy a fault-tolerant quantum computer in Illinois in 2027.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment for INFQ shifted to ‘extremely bullish’ from ‘bullish’ and the ticker trended among the top five as of late Thursday.
“$INFQ regardless of temporary price movement, this news is yet more indication that this company underpromises and over delivers,” a trader wrote.
”In a world built mostly on hype these days, INFQ continues to take a conservative approach to goal setting and routinely delivers more in less time than the stated goal.”
Infleqtion is the first neutral-atom quantum computing company to go public. In its February SPAC merger, the company raised more than $550 million in gross proceeds.

The prominent overclocker has revealed why the RTX 3090 Ti KINGPIN was facing a problem with its production.
Overclocker KINGPIN Says NVIDIA's Limitation on Using Single 12VHPWR Connector on RTX 3090 Ti KINGPIN "Screwed up the Production Timeline"
The legendary overclocker Vince "KINGPIN" Lucido has uploaded his very first video on his new YouTube channel called Overclock Kingpin, where he announces that he is working with ASUS. In the video, Vince showed off some hardware sent by ASUS for testing, but he also talked about some previous issues he faced while working at EVGA.
We know that the EVGA and NVIDIA relationship couldn't last long and ended in 2022 when the board partner couldn't sustain its GPU business, as NVIDIA's own Founders Edition cards were competing with EVGA's custom GPUs. At the same time, NVIDIA wanted EVGA to price the budget GPUs lower to the point where the company was selling its GPUs at a loss.
Vince said that when it came to the production of EVGA's last flagship card, which was the EVGA RTX 3090 Ti KINGPIN Hybrid edition, NVIDIA messed up the production line, as Vince wanted the GPU to have dual 12VHPWR connections, while NVIDIA wanted to limit it to just one connector. The GPU eventually launched three months after the launch of the RTX 3090 Ti, but the production line was interrupted due to the connector issue.
Right before the 3090 Ti KINGPIN launched, NVIDIA tried to force us to use one power connector on the card and it really screwed the production timeline up of my card and it actually ended up being severely limited because of it. I just think if you’re going to spend 5,000 plus on a card, you should really be able to do with it what you want.
- Vince KINGPIN Lucido
This also resulted in fewer units being produced and was the last flagship NVIDIA GPU EVGA ever made. The RTX 3090 Ti was launched at a hefty price tag of $1,999, and the RTX 3090 Ti KINGPIN Hybrid card with dual 12-pin connectors launched at $2,500, bundled with a 1600W PSU. articles.title: SpaceX's $40 Billion AI Gambit Turns Satellites Into Flying Data Centers - ad-hoc-news.de
articles.summary: SpaceX's $40 Billion AI Gambit Turns Satellites Into Flying Data Centers  ad-hoc-news.de
articles.full_text:
SpaceX is quietly rewriting what it means to be a space company. The rocket launches that built its reputation are now the supporting act for something far larger: a plan to fuse orbital logistics, satellite broadband and artificial intelligence into a single infrastructure machine — one that would need capital on a scale rarely seen outside the largest hyperscalers.
At the center of that shift is a financing package still under negotiation. According to reports from Reuters and the Financial Times, SpaceX is in talks to raise $40 billion in debt to fund Nvidia AI chips. Roughly $10 billion of that would come through bank loans, with the remaining $30 billion raised via investment-grade bonds. The company has not confirmed the discussions, but the size alone signals intent: moving beyond pure transport in low Earth orbit toward serious computing capacity.
Why a rocket builder needs hyperscaler-grade silicon
The logic becomes clearer when the company's business lines are viewed together rather than in isolation. More than 11,000 Starlink satellites are already active, and the first 26 units of the new V3 generation reached orbit in late September. That expanding constellation generates a torrent of data that has to be routed, managed and protected in real time.
The congestion risk is no longer theoretical. Michael Nicolls, a senior manager at SpaceX, on Tuesday called for better data exchange and tighter maneuver coordination after satellites from different operators came close to one another. Autonomous collision avoidance and routing networks are computationally expensive problems — exactly the kind of workload that demands high-performance semiconductors.
A parallel build-out in mobile connectivity adds another layer. The FCC has already granted approval for a constellation of 15,000 direct-to-device satellites, and SpaceX's agreed acquisition of a nationwide 800 MHz spectrum portfolio from Grain Management — covering up to 14 MHz of paired spectrum — would give the satellite network a terrestrial footing. The goal is to establish Starlink Mobile as a meaningful US carrier.
Taken together, these threads point in one direction: satellites are no longer passive relay stations. They are becoming orbiting data centers, and the chip bill reflects that.
Wall Street reprices the story
Analysts have been quick to adjust. Goldman Sachs lifted its price target on October 5 from $220 to $230 while keeping a Buy rating, citing stronger forecasts for the AI segment and long-term launch opportunities. Barclays initiated coverage on Thursday with an Overweight rating and a $254 target. Susquehanna raised its target on October 7 from $144 to $173 but stayed at Hold. Morgan Stanley weighed in on October 6 with an Outperform rating and a $300 target; analyst Adam Jonas flagged the upcoming Starship Flight 15 test as a key catalyst and pointed to potential profit opportunities in artificial intelligence.
The stock closed Friday at €145.20, up 14% over 30 days, though it sits roughly 25% below its 52-week high of €194.46. Market capitalization stands at approximately €1,970.64 billion.
The launch business still pays the bills
None of the AI ambition would be credible without the operational record underneath it. On Saturday, a Falcon 9 lifted 21 data transport satellites for the US Space Development Agency from Vandenberg Air Force Base, expanding the military's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture. Days earlier, SpaceX wrapped up NASA's Crew-12 mission, with the capsule splashing down off the California coast.
The cadence continues. On October 13, the company plans to launch the CRS-35 cargo mission to the International Space Station for NASA, with a window around 6:33 a.m. ET. At Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A, preparations for future Starship flights are transitioning from construction to operational testing.
Government contracts of this kind provide steady revenue — the foundation on which capital-intensive ventures can be built. It is a model that pairs physical cargo capacity in orbit with the next wave of digital infrastructure.
Regulatory gates and the debt question
Not everything runs on schedule. Starship's development consumes enormous resources and depends on regulatory sign-offs. The FAA is currently conducting an environmental review for planned Starship and Super Heavy operations at Launch Complex SLC-37, with public comments accepted until October 14, 2026, before a license modification could clear the way for commercial launches and landings.
The bigger open question for investors is whether a privately held space company can carry a debt load of this magnitude without losing operational flexibility. If the chip financing materializes, SpaceX would cement a position that neither pure rocket builders nor pure telecom operators can match — a bet on total connectivity, with the upside that implies and the risks of a heavily leveraged balance sheet to match.

articles.full_text:
Synopsis
In March, US prosecutors charged Ting-Wei "Willy" Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder, with conspiring to divert about $2.5 billion worth of US AI technology to China in violation of export laws.
The court docket showed Sun entered his guilty plea on Thursday in US District Court in Manhattan.
Super Micro did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment. It shares were down marginally in extended trading.
The alleged scheme began around 2024, with the defendants accused of using a company in Southeast Asia as a pass-through entity to conceal the China-based end customers, according to the indictment.
The United States and China are competing for dominance in artificial intelligence, with both investing billions of dollars in a technology seen as critical to economic growth, national security and military and cybersecurity capabilities.
Washington has tightened export controls, restricting sales of advanced AI chips and server systems to China without a licence, citing national security concerns.
The indictment said Nvidia's B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, are on the Commerce Control List and subject to the restrictions.

articles.title: Super Micro-Linked Contractor Pleads Guilty in $2.5bn Nvidia AI Chip Smuggling Scheme to China - Tekedia
articles.summary: Super Micro-Linked Contractor Pleads Guilty in $2.5bn Nvidia AI Chip Smuggling Scheme to China  Tekedia
articles.full_text:
A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer has pleaded guilty to participating in a scheme to illegally export advanced artificial intelligence servers containing Nvidia chips to China, adding a criminal conviction to a case that has placed a major AI hardware supplier and Washington’s technology export controls under scrutiny.
Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods out of the United States, defraud the government and obstruct justice. He entered the plea on Thursday in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, according to a court filing made public on Friday.
The case stems from a broader alleged operation in which Sun and two other individuals associated with Super Micro were accused of conspiring to divert approximately $2.5 billion worth of US artificial intelligence technology to China in violation of export laws.

Prosecutors charged the three men in March, alleging that the scheme began around October 2023 and involved exporting servers from a US manufacturer, widely believed to be Super Micro, to China without the required licenses.
The guilty plea marks a significant development in the case, which concerns technology at the center of the intensifying competition between Washington and Beijing for leadership in artificial intelligence. Advanced AI chips and the servers that house them are critical to training and running powerful models, while also supporting applications with potential national security and military implications.
Super Micro, based in California, said it had previously stated that it was not named as a defendant in the indictment and that the case had not affected its business operations. The company terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year.
The indictment identified Sun as a broker and “fixer” who allegedly helped facilitate orders and conceal the export operation. Prosecutors said he worked with others to arrange the shipment of servers containing advanced computing hardware to China without the necessary US authorization.
The equipment allegedly involved Nvidia’s B200, H100, and H200 graphics processing units, which Washington has subjected to export restrictions. The controls are intended to limit China’s access to advanced computing technology that US officials consider sensitive because of its potential applications in artificial intelligence development and national security.
The indictment alleged that Sun helped stage “dummy” servers in December 2025 to conceal the diversion of the equipment. It also accused him of making false statements to a US Department of Commerce officer during an inspection of servers that were supposedly being stored but had already been diverted to China.
Those allegations formed part of the case against Sun and his co-defendants. His guilty plea establishes his admission of guilt on the four counts to which he pleaded, while the status and outcome of the charges against the other defendants remain separate matters.
The alleged use of staged servers illustrates the enforcement challenge facing US authorities as they attempt to prevent restricted hardware from reaching prohibited destinations through intermediaries, complex sales arrangements and misleading documentation.
Export controls can restrict direct sales of advanced processors to certain buyers, but enforcement also depends on identifying the final destination of equipment, verifying its end use, and detecting attempts to conceal where products are being shipped. Server systems matter because they package high-performance chips into computing infrastructure that can be deployed at scale.
For AI developers, access to large clusters of advanced processors can determine how quickly they can train sophisticated models and expand their computing capacity. This makes high-end chips and AI servers commercially valuable, while increasing the incentives for buyers to seek access to restricted hardware through alternative channels.
Sun was a contractor associated with Super Micro. The other defendants named in the March indictment were Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw, a co-founder of the AI-server maker, and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, a sales manager at the company’s Taiwan office.
Liaw co-founded Super Micro in 1993 and joined its board in 2023.
The allegations have drawn attention to the position of Super Micro within the AI infrastructure supply chain. The company manufactures server systems used to deploy advanced processors, including Nvidia GPUs, and operates in a market benefiting from heavy investment in AI computing capacity.
Super Micro has sought to distinguish itself from the criminal allegations, stating that it was not named as a defendant in the indictment and that the matter had not affected its business operations. Its decision to terminate Sun and sever ties with the other defendants earlier this year also marked its response to the case.
The indictment does not, by itself, establish that Super Micro as a corporate entity committed the alleged offences.
Nevertheless, cases involving employees, contractors or senior figures linked to technology suppliers can raise questions about internal controls, customer verification and oversight of transactions involving restricted equipment. For companies operating across international supply chains, compliance failures can carry legal and reputational consequences even where corporate criminal liability has not been established.
The prosecution also highlights the challenge of policing AI hardware flows at a time when global demand for computing infrastructure is rising rapidly. Suppliers must navigate licensing requirements and restrictions that can vary according to chip performance, destination, end user, and intended application.
US-China AI Rivalry Drives Tighter Technology Controls
The case unfolds against a broader geopolitical contest in which the United States and China are investing billions of dollars in AI systems viewed as important to economic competitiveness, technological leadership and military capabilities.
Washington has tightened restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China, seeking to limit access to computing resources that could support the development of powerful AI models and sensitive military applications. Nvidia’s high-performance processors have become a focal point of those restrictions because of their role in modern AI training and inference.
The restrictions have created a difficult environment for chipmakers and server manufacturers, which must balance commercial demand against US rules governing exports to particular markets. They have also increased the importance of compliance throughout the distribution chain, from manufacturers and resellers to brokers and other intermediaries.
The alleged $2.5 billion diversion scheme underlines the scale of the potential stakes. If advanced computing equipment is redirected through unauthorized channels, it can undermine the practical effect of restrictions even when formal licensing rules remain in place.
At the same time, the prosecution does not establish how much of the allegedly diverted equipment ultimately reached particular Chinese customers or what AI applications it may have supported. The $2.5 billion figure refers to the technology prosecutors alleged the defendants conspired to divert, rather than a judicial finding that every part of that amount was successfully smuggled into China.
Sun’s guilty plea is therefore a concrete development in a wider enforcement effort, but the case against the other defendants and the full scope of the alleged operation remain important to its eventual outcome.
For the AI industry, the implications extend beyond the individuals charged. As advanced computing hardware becomes more valuable to both commercial AI development and national security, US authorities are seeking to ensure that export restrictions apply not only on paper but across the networks through which chips and server systems are sold and delivered.

articles.title: University of Saskatchewan Researchers Achieve Record Hyperbolic Surface Code Efficiency for Modular Fault-Tolerant Architectures - Quantum Computing Report
articles.summary: University of Saskatchewan Researchers Achieve Record Hyperbolic Surface Code Efficiency for Modular Fault-Tolerant Architectures  Quantum Computing Report
articles.full_text:
In a research paper published on arXiv, researchers Ahmed Adel Mahmoud and Dr. Steven Rayan from the Centre for Quantum Topology and Its Applications (quanTA) at the University of Saskatchewan have demonstrated explicit finite families of geometry-optimized hyperbolic surface codes that attain the optimal efficiency scaling limit set by Delfosse’s bound (η = kd2/n ∝ (log k)2).
By embedding quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) interactions onto compactified hyperbolic surfaces and optimizing periodic boundary conditions, the team doubled code distance and quadrupled efficiency without increasing qubit counts or check weights. Among the discovered families, the optimal {6, 6} code [[51330, 17112, 10]] encodes 17,112 logical qubits into 51,330 physical qubits with a record efficiency of η ≈ 33.34—a 33-fold gain over standard 2D toric codes.
To address physical hardware limits, the authors created a compiler that partitions these codes into planar modules of 80 or fewer qubits per chip. Circuit-level simulations under an SI1000-like noise model showed robust thresholds of approximately 0.22%, holding at 0.17% even when inter-module CNOT error rates were tripled.
| [ Key Quantum Error Correction Parameters ] |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Parameter | Name | Definition & Operational Meaning | 
| • n | • Physical Qubits | • The total count of raw hardware qubits built onto the processing chip. | 
| • k | • Logical Qubits | • The number of error-protected qubits bundled together to run computations. | 
| • d | • Code Distance | • The minimum physical errors needed to corrupt a logical qubit. Higher is better. | 
| • η = kd2/n | • Code Efficiency | • The ratio measuring logical protection (k, d) achieved per physical qubit (n). | 
What This Discovery Means in Plain English
Think of physical qubits as fragile glass ornaments and quantum noise as accidental bumps. Standard quantum error correction protects one ornament by wrapping it in a massive box of foam peanuts (physical qubits), making large systems resource-intensive. The Saskatchewan team designed a curved, multi-dimensional geometric “box” that wraps thousands of ornaments together using shared connections. They also developed a method to slice this curved pattern into tiny, flat 80-qubit microchips, letting future quantum computers run thousands of protected operations with a fraction of the hardware.

articles.title: As Musk takes on Ambani, here's what's keeping Starlink's India ambitions in limbo - Invezz
articles.summary: As Musk takes on Ambani, here's what's keeping Starlink's India ambitions in limbo  Invezz
articles.full_text:
powered by
Buy Reliance Industries (Jio) on the view that India’s satellite approvals keep shifting toward domestic champions: Jio already has a clear path with IN-SPACe deeming its LEO plan “technically sound,” plus it’s the retail distribution partner for Starlink hardware. If Starlink stays stuck on spectrum/ground/security steps, Jio captures the “universal connectivity” demand with its own network and keeps the Starlink retail option as a fallback.
Key Risk: A fast Starlink commercial launch in India that forces Jio to cut prices and lose enterprise/remote-site share before Jio’s LEO rollout monetizes.
Buy Eutelsat (via Eutelsat Group) because India’s regulator says all three licensees are at the same stage, and Eutelsat/OneWeb is already structurally positioned as a non-US alternative with Bharti backing. If Starlink’s political friction drags, India’s satellite broadband market still needs capacity—OneWeb can win early tenders for enterprise connectivity and government-adjacent projects once spectrum assignment completes.
Key Risk: India delays spectrum assignment or security assessments longer than expected specifically for OneWeb/Eutelsat, leaving it stuck without revenue while Starlink eventually launches.
- Musk alleges Ambani is influencing India's Starlink approval process.
- Starlink, Reliance Jio and Eutelsat's OneWeb are awaiting security clearances.
- Security, concerns over dependence on a foreign satellite network remain key challenges.
SpaceX chief Elon Musk's years-long effort to bring its satellite internet service Starlink to India took a dramatic turn this week.
Musk, whose company competes with Ambani's Reliance Jio and Eutelsat's OneWeb in India's satellite communications market, on Thursday took to X, the social media platform he owns, to challenge the delay in Starlink's commercial launch.
Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license? Is Ambani the real boss of India?
The government is more interested in protecting the interests of crony capitalists than of citizens
"Starlink is licensed in over 165 countries and has spent five years complying with every single law and requirement of the government of India, so why still no license?
Is Ambani the real boss of India?"
The combative remarks came a day after Musk was more indirect in his attack against what he claims is obstructing his entry into the Indian market.
"Unfortunately, we are being blocked by certain oligarchs in order to maintain their monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people. You can guess who they are …
This is a crime against the people of India!" he said on X on Wednesday.
The comments have brought the rivalry between two of the world's wealthiest businessmen into the open again, placing renewed attention on India's regulatory approach to satellite broadband and the commercial stakes involved in opening one of the world's largest internet markets to Starlink.
Starlink received a licence to launch commercial operations in India last year, clearing a major regulatory hurdle for the satellite provider, which has been pursuing entry into the country since 2022.
It became the third company to receive India's approval to provide satellite communications services, following clearances for Eutelsat's OneWeb and Reliance Jio.
However, the licence did not automatically allow Starlink to begin commercial operations.
The company must still secure spectrum from the government, establish ground infrastructure and demonstrate through testing and trials that it complies with the security requirements it has agreed to meet.
India's telecom ministry rejects Musk's allegations
India's ministry of communications was quick to respond to Musk's criticism, rejecting suggestions that the regulatory framework was being applied unfairly or that Starlink was being treated differently from its domestic competitors.
The ministry said telecom licences had been granted to three providers of Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite services based on non-geosynchronous satellite orbit technology.
However, it said each licensee was required to demonstrate compliance with security conditions intended to ensure that its services met the necessary requirements for protecting users and their data.
"Security assessment as part of this process is currently under way in respect of all the three licensees. As and when this process is completed for a licensed entity, it may proceed to the next step of seeking assignment of spectrum. At present, all the three entities are at broadly the same regulatory stage. As such, the suggestion that the framework or its application is unfair or discriminatory is baseless and misconceived," the ministry said.
"Waiting for our own approvals", say competitors
The dispute unfolded even as senior executives from Starlink, Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel gathered at the India Mobile Congress in New Delhi, where the companies discussed their plans for satellite internet services.
Akash Ambani, chairman of Reliance Jio Infocomm and son of Mukesh Ambani, said the company was developing its own satellite communications technology and working towards securing regulatory approvals.
Asked by a reporter about Musk's allegations, Akash declined to comment directly, saying only: "We want to be heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Then, on the sidelines of the event, Sunil Mittal, chairman of Bharti Enterprises and the largest shareholder in the Eutelsat group, also said the company was waiting for the necessary approvals.
Eutelsat is the French satellite operator that merged with the UK's OneWeb, which is backed by the Bharti group.
"We're waiting for our own approvals," Mittal said, adding that the group's satellite services would begin "hopefully soon" in India.
Musk's comments also came hours after Lauren Dreyer, Starlink's vice president of business operations, appeared at the India Mobile Congress.
"We stand ready to serve India," Dreyer said, adding that Starlink wanted to help realise Prime Minister Narendra Modi's goal of achieving universal connectivity across the country.
The seeds of the Musk-Ambani rivalry
The latest episode is only another chapter in the complicated relationship between Musk and Ambani, both of whom are eyeing to establish themselves as the go-to players in India's satellite internet market.
The seeds of the rivalry were first sown when Musk sought entry into the Indian market and argued that satellite spectrum should be assigned administratively, in line with the approach followed in several other countries.
Reliance, meanwhile, argued that the spectrum should be auctioned to ensure a level playing field between satellite operators and traditional telecommunications companies.
Starlink lobbied the Indian government against an auction, arguing that satellite spectrum was a natural resource that should be shared among companies rather than allocated through a competitive bidding process.
An auction could impose geographical restrictions and increase costs, the company argued in letters made public by the Indian government, Reuters reported.
Musk said a decision by India to auction satellite broadband spectrum rather than allocate it administratively would be "unprecedented".
In 2024, India's government sided with Musk on the spectrum allocation question, deciding that satellite broadband spectrum would be assigned administratively rather than through an auction.
Musk welcomed the decision, saying on X: "We will do our best to serve the people of India with Starlink".
There was also speculation among some observers that expediting Starlink's entry could help India strengthen its trade relationship with the US administration.
Some Indian government officials were reported anonymously to have viewed faster approvals as potentially helpful in broader trade negotiations.
The timing of the current dispute also adds a diplomatic dimension, as New Delhi and Washington have struggled to finalise a trade deal after reaching a framework in February.
Then, last year, in a surprise move, Reliance Jio signed a deal with Musk's SpaceX to bring Starlink satellite internet services to India.
Under the arrangement, India's largest telecom operator would stock Starlink equipment in its retail stores, giving the satellite company access to thousands of outlets across the country.
Nevertheless, the latest exchange shows that disagreements over market access and regulatory treatment remain unresolved.
Why India needs satellite internet
India represents an important opportunity for Starlink because of its large internet-connected population and the persistent gaps in broadband infrastructure outside major urban centres.
The country had 1,065.88 million broadband internet subscribers at the end of March 2026, making it the world's second-largest internet market by connected population, behind China.
Mobile wireless connections accounted for more than 94% of India's internet subscriptions, reflecting the country's reliance on mobile networks rather than fixed-line broadband.
"This means that India's digital economy is 'mobile-first,' with substantial gaps in wired broadband, especially in rural areas. In other words, as one moves away from major urban centers, the internet infrastructure for industrial applications remains underdeveloped. The reliability of wireless connections is patchy at best, and fixed broadband speeds are dismally low," wrote Trisha Ray, associate director and resident fellow at the Atlantic Council.
The government has attempted to address these shortcomings through BharatNet, an initiative housed under the public sector telecommunications company BSNL.

articles.title: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules - BBC
articles.summary: Prize-winning image which sparked backlash was AI-generated, Nikon rules  BBCBig Controversy Upends a Contest About Microscopic Videos  The New York TimesAI disqualification yields new Nikon Small World in Motion winner  Ars TechnicaContest-Winning Microscope Video Thrown Out for Using Generative AI  GizmodoTop Science Photography Award Winner Stripped For AI Use  Yahoo
articles.full_text:
The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified following concerns raised by other scientists that it was fake.
Nikon said the use of generative AI in the composition of the video broke the rules of its Small World In Motion contest, which accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes.
The firm said the video "did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI", but added it was not a judgement of the entrant's professional reputation or scientific contributions.
It said it would now look at the rules and procedures of the annual contest, which has been running for 15 years and is specifically for microscopic images.
Nikon said it came to the decision "after thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel".
The winning entry came from Dr Ning Xu, from Tsinghua University in China, who submitted a short video showing tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving in the airway of a child with the respiratory condition PCD.
The BBC has approached him for comment.
A number of scientists, including former competition judges, complained to Nikon on its LinkedIn page that the video did not appear to be real.
Xu had acknowledged using AI, but said he believed he had acted within the rules, and had cooperated with Nikon's investigation.
University of Leicester scientist Dr Robert Hirst, who was among the first experts to voice concerns, said he was "not surprised" and he "knew immediately that the video was fabricated".
"I have been diagnosing PCD for 20 years by examining their cilia waveform, length, cell size and shape," he said.
Hirst, who is lead scientist for the NHS centre for PCD diagnosis at the university, said the cells and cilia "look nothing like those from PCD patients".
"This controversy has impacted a lot of patients, scientists, doctors and PCD support networks around the world," he said.

articles.title: Review: 4-hour Musk documentary feels like two different films
articles.summary: Alex Gibney's provocative film is compelling but overlong, and there's not much new here for Ars readers.
articles.full_text:
Elon Musk is a very familiar figure to Ars readers, given his massive influence (for better and worse) on the technology sector over the last 20 years. Oscar-winning director Alex Gibney's latest biographical documentary—simply titled Musk—covers a lot of well-known ground and challenges the carefully crafted public image of Musk as a visionary tech titan.
Gibney's documentary presents Musk as more of a Gilded Age confidence man, rejiggered for the 21st century: an investor cosplaying as an inventor whose real genius is pumping stocks and dazzling investors and the public alike with visions of a high-tech utopian future. The film is bound to push all the right outrage buttons, whether one is a Musk fan or a detractor—which makes it very much a product of the peculiar social media-driven era in which we live.
Gibney has been making documentaries since the 1980s, covering such varied subjects as Jimi Hendrix, Hunter S. Thompson and gonzo journalism, WikiLeaks, Scientology, Steve Jobs, Elizabeth Holmes (the subject of another forthcoming documentary, You Can See Everything, featuring comedian Nathan Fielder), Boris Becker, The Sopranos creator David Chase, alleged Russian interference in the US 2016 presidential election, the opioid epidemic, and cyclist Lance Armstrong. He snagged his first Oscar nomination for 2005’s Enron: The Smartest Guys in the Room, and won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature two years later for Taxi to the Dark Side.Read full article

articles.title: Prime Video unveils Blade Runner 2099 full trailer at NYCC
articles.summary: Also: new trailer for Godzilla Minus Zero, the sequel to Takashi Yamazaki’s kaiju epic Godzilla Minus One
articles.full_text:
We got our first look at Prime Video's new sci-fi series Blade Runner 2099 in July at San Diego Comic-Con. With the show's premiere roughly six weeks away, the streamer unveiled the full trailer this weekend at New York Comic-Con. Co-stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer (Euphoria) joined showrunner Silka Luisa (Shining Girls) onstage for the big reveal.
As Luisa described the show during the NYCC panel Saturday night:
We are 50 years after [Blade Runner] 2049 and, bad news, the worst has happened. The replicant uprising that has been bubbling up in the films has taken place and the humans have lost. So the creations have surpassed their creators. And the series, the big question it asks is, ‘What happens when our time as a species ends?’ 2099 is taking place at a junction point when one species is ending and a new one is rising. The first film, something I loved about it, was that it was looking at mortality on a micro level. Roy Batty and the other replicants were fighting for more life. This show asks that same question but on a macro level. Mankind—what happens when we realize our time is running out? And are we going to accept that loss? Can we hold on to our humanity during it?
Yeoh stars as Olwen, the dying Replicant, while Schafer plays Cora. The cast also includes Hugo Hamlet as Buster Friendly, as well as Dmitri Abold, Lewis Gribben, Katelyn Rose Downey, Daniel Rigby, Johnny Harris, Amy Lennox, Sheila Atim, Matthew Needham, Tom Burke, and Maurizio Lombardi—all in as-yet-undisclosed roles.Read full article

articles.title: One with the world? A new look at brains transformed by psychedelics.
articles.summary: Participants meditated inside an MRI tube, with and without psilocybin.
articles.full_text:
For about a decade, the mainstream understanding has been that psychedelics cause chaos in the brain. Brain networks—the stable patterns of communication that handle vision, attention, or our sense of self, and more—loosen and start talking to each other all at once. EEG traces get noisier and more complex. “Think of the networks of the brain as highways,” says Devon Stoliker, a neuroscientist at Monash University. “Under psychedelics, these highways break down into many different directions.”
In a recent Nature study, Stoliker’s team designed an experiment to test whether these directions are truly chaotic and random. Researchers gathered 62 people who had never taken a psychedelic before, gave them 19 milligrams of psilocybin, a common psychedelic found in certain fungi, and scanned their brains. Then, they used AI to analyze the drugged and sober brain scans. What emerged was not exactly chaos.
An uninterrupted trip
Stoliker thinks chaos is not a satisfactory explanation for psychedelics’ effect on the brain. “It never really explained why an individual would have a meaningful experience, why they might have insight, why they might experience clarity, and why these might translate into positive psychological changes,” Stoliker says. To investigate if there are other explanations, he and his colleagues designed a study called PsiConnect.Read full article
